name: Transifex
tagline: Manage a small software localization project with translation memory and review

pricing.notes: Typical Starter monthly package; seat and word limits apply.

tiers.name: Starter
tiers.limits: 10 collaborators; unlimited projects/files; price rises across hosted-word bands (monthly table lists $160, $260, $380 and $510)
tiers.notes: Lowest published band shown; annual bands are $135, $215, $320 and $425 per month.

tiers.name: Growth
tiers.limits: 30 collaborators; annual plan includes 60,000 AI words/year; price rises across hosted-word bands up to $2,465 monthly
tiers.notes: Lowest published band shown; annual bands start at $200/mo and rise to $2,050/mo.

tiers.name: Enterprise+
tiers.limits: 100 collaborators; annual plan includes 300,000 AI words/year; up to 6 TB/year Transifex Live usage
tiers.notes: Contact sales; malformed placeholder prices on page were not treated as real.

pricing.freeTierCaps: no general free tier; free trial only, plus a separate free program for qualifying non-commercial open-source projects
pricing.hiddenCosts: Base price scales by hosted-word band; AI capacity is a paid add-on from $84/month for Starter and monthly subscribers; LexiQA and some support/onboarding capabilities are add-ons.

verdictSummary: A consolation build is possible, but the paid product's decisive value sits outside a solo rebuild. For Transifex, manage a small software localization project with translation memory and review. The hard boundary is enterprise workflows, integrations, continuous localization, vendors, and support, plus translation memory, collaboration, and deployment integrations.
coreLoopDIY: Manage translation keys for a small software localization project with translation memory and review, preserve context, import and export standard files, and publish approved strings.
requirements: optional DeepL or OpenAI API key
whatYouLose: enterprise workflows, integrations, continuous localization, vendors, and support
moatNotes: translation memory, collaboration, and deployment integrations
ongoingBurden: file formats, placeholders, plural rules, screenshots, context, permissions, review, glossary, machine translation, sync, and backups
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Transifex because localization teams pay because language context, review discipline, translators, and release integrations are the hard parts. The recurring cost buys file formats, placeholders, plural rules, screenshots, context, permissions, review, glossary, machine translation, sync, and backups, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Tolgee
priorArt.desc: Active open-source localization platform with translation memory and in-context tooling.

alternatives.name: Tolgee
alternatives.desc: In-context product localization with memory, terminology and review, sized sensibly for a small team.

facts.install: Hosted Tolgee Cloud signup or the official Docker Compose deployment with PostgreSQL
facts.engines: Tolgee's contextual AI translator and machine-translation layer can connect to Google Cloud Translation, Amazon Translate, DeepL, Microsoft Azure Translator, Baidu, and configured LLM/MT providers.
facts.dataFormat: Self-hosted projects, keys, translations, users, and translation memory live in PostgreSQL, while screenshots and uploaded files live under the persistent data directory; cloud accounts store the same classes of data on Tolgee infrastructure.
facts.gapVsPaid: Tolgee is easier for in-context product strings but has a narrower enterprise integration, content-delivery, analytics, vendor, and workflow layer than Transifex.
facts.setupBlocker: None for cloud signup; self-hosting needs Docker, an external PostgreSQL database, persistent file storage, mail/domain/TLS, backups, and provider keys for third-party translation engines.

alternatives.name: Weblate
alternatives.desc: A mature continuous-localization system with source-control sync, translation memory, checks and review.

facts.install: Hosted Weblate signup or the official Docker Compose deployment
facts.engines: Machine translation can connect to OpenAI/Azure OpenAI, DeepL, Google Cloud, Amazon Translate, Microsoft Translator, LibreTranslate, Baidu, Yandex, and other documented services.
facts.dataFormat: Translations, users, review state, memory, glossaries, and settings live in PostgreSQL; cloned source repositories and uploaded files live in persistent server volumes, with Valkey/Redis used for queues and caches.
facts.gapVsPaid: Weblate excels at repository-driven software translation but lacks Transifex's polished hosted content delivery, broader business integrations, vendor workflow, and low-admin onboarding.
facts.setupBlocker: Cloud hosting is free only for qualifying libre projects; the general free route requires Docker, PostgreSQL, Valkey/Redis, domain/TLS, mail, repository credentials, backups, and upgrades.

alternatives.name: Mozilla Pontoon
alternatives.desc: A proven software-localization workspace with repository sync and peer review, but no turnkey little-team deployment.

facts.install: Docker setup is documented for development; production deployment must be adapted from Mozilla/Heroku-style infrastructure
facts.dataFormat: Projects sync translations to version-control repositories, while users, suggestions, reviews, translation memory, and job state live in Pontoon's server databases and caches; Mozilla's public instance is not a general hosted service.
facts.gapVsPaid: Pontoon is not a turnkey small-team service and gives up Transifex's hosted reliability, commercial support, content delivery, integration catalog, and configurable workflows.
facts.setupBlocker: The first obstacle is that the official Docker stack is explicitly not for production and the project does not provide a turnkey supported deployment for arbitrary operators.

alternatives.name: Accent
alternatives.desc: String collaboration, history, review and automation in a leaner package than Transifex's expanding universe.

facts.install: Run the published Docker image with an external PostgreSQL database and production environment variables
facts.dataFormat: Projects, languages, strings, translations, comments, history, and users live in PostgreSQL; application configuration and secrets live on the server.
facts.gapVsPaid: Accent's collaboration and history are useful, but its file-format breadth, translation memory, automation, integrations, permissions, and commercial support trail Transifex.
facts.setupBlocker: The first obstacle is a production Elixir web deployment with Docker, external PostgreSQL, SECRET_KEY_BASE and authentication configuration, TLS, mail, backups, and upgrades; the old standalone Accent CLI is archived.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Starter plan and a small-team string-management system DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a closest honest personal substitute for Transifex in an empty repository.
Use Next.js 15, TypeScript, PostgreSQL, Drizzle ORM, and one optional machine-translation API; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: manage translation keys for a small software localization project with translation memory and review, preserve context, import and export standard files, and publish approved strings.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Implement projects, locales, keys, namespaces, descriptions, screenshots, translations, and review status.
Import and export JSON, YAML, PO, and XLIFF while preserving placeholders and plural forms.
Add glossary checks, missing-string filters, translation memory, comments, and reviewer assignment.
Use machine translation only on selected strings and show provider, cost, and source text before approval.
Provide token-authenticated pull and push endpoints for CI with an immutable change log.
Add backups, locale deletion safeguards, and a pseudo-localization preview.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Do not claim to reproduce proprietary data, network liquidity, regulated access, or frontier infrastructure.
Deliberately leave out a translator labor marketplace.
Deliberately leave out a global website translation proxy.
Deliberately leave out enterprise integrations, legal translation assurance, and round-the-clock support.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
